Issued at 330 PM EDT Sun Oct 11 2026

This afternoon's GOES Channel 10 water vapor imagery shows what
remains of Isaias penetrating inland to Kentucky while a PNW 
low works with Tropical Storm Rachel to send moisture streaming 
northeast toward Ontario and Quebec. Locally, a weak, extended 
1005 mb pressure area approaches parallel to the northwestern 
shore of Lake Superior, and a slightly weakened (relative to 
yesterday) pressure gradient sits southwest to northeast across 
the CWA. GRB's 12Z sounding shows an entire column of 
substaintally dry air, including a 900 mb dewpoint depression 
near 25C. Still in a southerly flow regime with a relatively 
stacked pressure gradient, winds to 15-25 mph have been observed
across the UP today, with higher gusts in downloping areas 
along the Lake Superior shoreline up to 30-40mph. RH's recovered
well in the eastern UP and poorly in the west last night; 
values reached 80-95% from Dickinson to Luce County, including 
the southern half of Marquette, whereas the western UP 
(including the Keweenaw) reached RHs ranging from 50-65%. So far
today, RHs have decreased from there and currently sit at 
35-40% in the west and 45-60% in the east. Thus, with the HDW 
index sitting between the 75th and 90th percentiles for much of 
the UP today, elevated to critical fire weather conditions 
continue to manifest. A Red Flag Warning is still in effect for 
Gogebic and Ontonagon Counties until 5 pm CDT today.

Tonight begins shifting patterns toward cooler, wetter conditions, 
which should be realized starting Monday night. As high pressure 
from the northern Canadian provinces fills in and Isaias shifts east 
toward the DC area, the elongated low dissipates southeastward 
across the the Upper Great Lakes for the remainder of today and into 
tomorrow. As this low center drops toward lower Michigan, its place 
is taken up by a Plains low tracking east along the southern edge of 
the Canadian high pressure. This means elevated surface winds 
diminish into the evening today, until northeasterly flow kicks in 
tomorrow with the approach of the second low from the southeast. 
Highs tomorrow remain anomalously high (15-20 above normal, except 
for the Keweenaw, which achieves only climate normal) in the mid to 
high 70s (50s Keweenaw), and lows tomorrow should be likewise warm 
in the mid 40s to high 50s (cooler in the Keweenaw). Tuesday at last 
sees the effects of CAA, with highs in the 50s and 60s -- comparable 
to tonight's lows! 

Monday evening also heralds the arrival of some light precipitation. 
The plume of Pacific moisture works its way south, and the area may 
see light rain starting Monday evening (sooner at Isle Royale and 
the Keweenaw) and continuing into Tuesday morning. Subsequent NBM 
runs have steadily inched 24-hour QPF totals up, with most of the 
rain manifesting over Lake Superior, Isle Royale, and the Keweenaw. 
For the bulk of the UP, though, probabilities of greater than 0.25" 
of rain ending at 8 AM Tuesday morning now stand between 25-65%, 
being greater the farther north. A few rumbles of thunder are 
possible overnight Monday, too.

High pressure moves in Wednesday, bringing a return to dry weather 
while temperatures trend more seasonal. Towards the latter half of 
the work week, the general setup among deterministic and ensemble 
guidance is for another midlevel low to close off and spin over the 
Rockies while a deepening trough drops out of Alberta. And this is 
where the similarities end, with some of the guidance showing a 
phasing of these two systems and a deep low pressure system moving 
over the UP, while other guidance just brings the more northern wave 
through. This all brings the potential for more rounds of wet 
weather into the forecast towards the end of the work week, as well 
as a shot of colder air into the weekend, though confidence in the 
finer points is low.
